title: Saturn’s rings are 280,000 km wide but often just 10 m thick
body: Saturn’s main rings stretch roughly 280,000 km from edge to edge, more than 20 Earths side by side, yet in places they are estimated to be only about 10 metres thick. They are made of countless chunks of almost pure water ice, each on its own orbit around the planet. Shrink the rings to the thickness of a sheet of paper and they would still be nearly 3 km wide.

slides.heading: Widths, side by side: which is widest?
slides.note: Edge to edge the rings span about 22 Earths, yet in places they are only about 10 m thick
slides.explanation: The rings would not quite reach from Earth to the Moon: 280,000 km against 384,400.

slides.heading: Dust to boulders
slides.text: Ring particles range from specks smaller than a grain of sand to chunks metres across, all orbiting Saturn like countless tiny moons.

slides.heading: Maybe surprisingly young
slides.text: Cassini data suggest the rings may be just 10 to 100 million years old, younger than the first dinosaurs, though their age is still debated.

slides.heading: Galileo’s vanishing act
slides.text: Galileo saw the rings as Saturn’s “ears”. In 1612 Earth lined up with the ring plane, they seemed to vanish, and he was baffled.

slides.question: Why did Saturn’s rings seem to vanish when Galileo looked in 1612?
options: Earth lined up with the ring plane
slides.explanation: The rings are incredibly thin, so when Earth lined up with the ring plane in 1612 they seemed to disappear. Galileo, who saw them as Saturn’s ‘ears’, was baffled.
